item.title: AI’s ability to find cyber flaws outpacing firms’ capacity to fix them: Palo Alto Networks' Nikesh Arora
item.description: Nikesh Arora, Chairman and CEO of Palo Alto Networks, has called for faster and more collaborative approaches to vulnerability management.
item.content:encoded:
Nikesh Arora, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Palo Alto Networks, has raised concerns about the growing use of frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models to identify software vulnerabilities and link them into potential attack paths. 

While these capabilities can help strengthen cybersecurity, they could also give attackers faster ways to exploit weaknesses in enterprise systems. The bigger challenge, Arora notes in a LinkedIn post, is ensuring that organisations can verify, prioritise and fix vulnerabilities at the same pace at which AI can discover them.

“Most organizations do not have capacity to patch at the speed needed, especially the smaller ones,” Arora wrote. Smaller businesses often lack security specialists, while larger ones must test fixes against existing applications. He also says models identify different weaknesses, so one model cannot provide complete coverage.

Finding a flaw is only the start. Teams must confirm it, assess the risk, develop a fix, test for disruption and deploy it. False positives, or incorrect alerts, waste time, while untested patches can disrupt services.

The scale is growing. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology said submissions to its National Vulnerability Database rose 263% between 2020 and 2025. It enriched nearly 42,000 records in 2025, but this was still insufficient. In April 2026, it adopted risk-based prioritisation, focusing on exploited flaws and critical software.

AI developers are linking discovery with repair. Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, launched in April 2026 with Palo Alto Networks among its partners, gives selected organisations access to Claude Mythos Preview for defensive security. Anthropic said partners had identified more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity flaws by June and expanded the programme to around 150 additional organisations. 

On November 4, OpenAI reported that a controlled Linux-kernel pipeline generated candidate patches for 948 local privilege-escalation vulnerabilities, which allow a user to gain higher access rights. Human researchers reviewed the findings before reporting them to maintainers.

In India, CERT-In’s November 4 advisory warned of an AI-assisted threat actor targeting non-bank lenders, fintech firms, payment providers and cryptocurrency platforms through machine intelligence and payment APIs. The agency has also issued 2026 guidance on AI-assisted vulnerability defence and AI security auditing.

Arora advocates virtual patching as an interim measure. “The most obvious solution is virtual patching. This is a time tested technology that is currently available with cyber vendors for endpoints, WAF, cloud, network use cases.” 

WAF is a web application firewall, which filters website and application traffic. A virtual patch is a security rule that blocks a known method of exploiting a flaw without changing the affected software. It buys time while a permanent update is tested, but does not remove the weakness. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project cautions that it protects only the traffic the system inspects and attacks variations its rules recognise.

Arora calls for a shared vulnerability clearing house and faster development of protective signatures, or detection rules. He also highlights operational technology, systems that monitor or control physical processes such as energy, water and transport. Patching them can be difficult because downtime may affect safety or essential services.

item.title: Workflow, AI, health: test your business creativity with Edition 257 of our weekly quiz!
item.description: This insightful feature from YourStory tests and strengthens your business acumen! Here are 5 questions to kick off this 257th quiz. Ready?
item.content:encoded:
Lateral Sparks, the weekly quiz from YourStory, tests your domain knowledge, business acumen, and lateral thinking skills (see the previous edition here). In this 257th edition of the quiz, we present issues tackled by real-life entrepreneurs in their startup journeys.

What would you do if you were in their shoes? At the end of the quiz, you will find out what the entrepreneurs and innovators themselves actually did. Would you do things differently?

Check out YourStory’s Book Review section as well, with takeaways from over 355 titles on creativity and entrepreneurship, and our weekend PhotoSparks section on creativity in the arts.

Also Read
Breaking barriers in 2025: Women’s progress at work and what the road ahead demands

Q1: Healthcare

The healthcare system is generally built to treat illness, not to find it early. Where are the entrepreneurial opportunities in preventive care at scale?

Q2: Elder care

Senior citizens today are unwilling to let age define how they live, and are looking for more quality of lifestyle. Where is the business opportunity here?

Also Read
Year in Review: Top 10 celebrity-backed ventures of 2025

Q3: Recycling

Efficient recycling of components in used objects can be complex in terms of determining what is inside, how much material can be recovered, and what it will cost to process. How can efficiency be improved here?

Q4: Social insights

Social media is a key discovery and evaluation channel for consumers, but brands don’t leverage these insights well. What can be done to deepen and apply business signals here?

Q5: Construction

Cost overruns, project delays, and disconnected processes remain major challenges in the construction industry. How can technology help here?

Answers!

Congratulations on having come this far! But there’s more to come – answers to these five questions (below), as well as links to articles with more details on the entrepreneurs’ solutions. Happy reading, happy learning – and happy creating!

A1: Healthcare

Founded by Shashank ND, Arpit Garg, and Anshul Khandelwal, healthtech startup Cent is building a vertically integrated preventive health platform. It combines customised hardware, AI-driven radiology, and bioinformatics.

It has reportedly completed 10,000 preventive whole-body scans in three cities since launch, and is targeting 10 million scans by 2035. Read more here about its disease detection capabilities, and its recent fundraise from Blume Ventures and South Park Commons.

A2: Elder care

Founded by Sharad Gadsing, Cradle Of Life focuses on offering seniors four fundamental human aspirations: freedom, purpose, health, and happiness. It enables seniors to learn, contribute and pursue what matters personally.

In terms of design, the residential facilities include a central balcony that extends to every room, layouts with more usable area, and safety through age-friendly furniture. Read more here about its other offerings in healthcare, emergency response, wellness, and community engagement.

Also Read
Year in review: startups that raised big from VCs in 2025

A3: Recycling

Attero is an e-waste and battery recycling company that uses AI to speed up decisions across thousands of appliances, suppliers and locations. It processes 200,000 metric tonnes of e-waste and 10,000 metric tonnes of lithium-ion batteries annually, according to Ayush Agarwal, Head of Product.

Its pricing engine combines material intelligence with market intelligence to calculate what the material should cost in a particular market. Read more here about its AI-powered compliance engine that checks documents, reconciles information across records, and flags exceptions.

A4: Social insights

“Brands today are drowning in signals and starved of action,” explains J Venkat, Co-founder of Live2.ai. It monitors conversations across Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, X, and review websites.

It integrates trend analysis, influencer-content audits, campaign publishing, and performance measurement for ecommerce. Read more here about how it serves more than 200 brands across the US, Europe and Southeast Asia.

Also Read
How IIT Madras Incubation Cell is powering India’s next-gen deeptech startups

A5: Construction

Founded by Saurav Bhaik and Ankit Sinha, ﻿Tagbin has developed an AI-powered product that integrates architectural drawings, mechanical systems, and project costing. The integrated workflow can be controlled through natural-language prompts.

The platform generates building models, incorporates applicable regulations, and creates construction schedules. Read more here about how it also takes soil-bearing strength and the water table into account while generating foundations and excavation plans.

YourStory has also published the pocketbook ‘Proverbs and Quotes for Entrepreneurs: A World of Inspiration for Startups’ as a creative and motivational guide for innovators.

item.title: How a Rs 500 Cr bet put Bihar Museum ahead of the Met and Louvre
item.description: How did Bihar Museum enter the global top 10? Shradha Sharma reflects on Nitish Kumar's vision, legal challenges and the persistence behind its success
item.content:encoded:
Bihar Museum in Patna was recently ranked ahead of New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Louvre in Paris. The museum has secured the ninth place on The World's 100 Best Museums 2026, published by German travel guide Worth a Journey. The Met stands tenth and the Louvre 31st. It is the only Indian institution on the list and the highest-ranked museum in Asia. For a museum that opened barely a decade ago, it is a significant achievement. More so because there was a time when the project itself faced serious opposition, with questions raised about its cost, relevance and the way it was being executed.

Reflecting on the recognition in a recent LinkedIn post, YourStory Founder and CEO Shradha Sharma recalled the roles played by two people in getting the museum built: Nitish Kumar, who championed the project as Bihar's Chief Minister, and 1992-batch IAS officer Chanchal Kumar, who was entrusted with its execution. When the state government proposed spending nearly Rs 500 crore on a world-class museum in Patna, the decision attracted criticism. Why should a state struggling with basic infrastructure invest so much in a museum? Who would visit it? Could the money have been better spent elsewhere? According to Sharma, even people within the political establishment questioned the proposal. Nitish Kumar, however, stood by the project, convinced that Bihar needed an institution worthy of its historical and cultural heritage.

This Diwali, this one is for everyone who has ever been written off.
A museum in Patna now ranks above the Met in New York and the Louvre in Paris. The Bihar Museum is 9th on the World’s 100 Best Museums list for 2026 put out by the German travel guide Worth a Journey. The Met is… pic.twitter.com/1sUAvkUqfh

— Shradha Sharma (@SharmaShradha) November 6, 2026

Getting the museum built

The challenges began with the land. According to Sharma, the proposed 13-acre site had seven government bungalows, some occupied by senior officials and a state minister. Getting the occupants to vacate required considerable administrative effort and legal intervention. She also recounted an incident in which men allegedly linked to local politicians entered the construction site demanding subcontracts, prompting police intervention. The museum was designed by Pritzker Prize-winning Japanese architect Fumihiko Maki in collaboration with Mumbai-based architectural firm Opolis, while Larsen & Toubro was selected to construct it. But appointing internationally recognised architects and an established construction company was only part of the challenge. Getting the project completed was another matter.

The museum also faced judicial scrutiny. In June 2015, the Patna High Court, hearing a public interest litigation, criticised the expenditure of approximately Rs 500 crore and questioned the transparency of the contracting process. The court held that the project was not in the public interest but declined to halt construction because the building was nearing completion. Those findings remain an important part of the museum's history. Its international recognition does not erase the questions raised about public spending and governance, although the institution has since gained recognition well beyond Bihar.

Sharma credits much of the execution to Chanchal Kumar, who held the dual responsibility of Secretary of Art and Culture and Secretary of the Building Construction Department.

The arrangement meant that both the museum's cultural vision and its construction came under the same officer. Sharma said she recently read his account of how the museum came together and was struck by how little he spoke about his own contribution. Behind the finished building were years of navigating approvals, land disputes, administrative resistance and the many complications that accompany a large public project. In Sharma's telling, Nitish Kumar's political backing and Chanchal Kumar's persistence were crucial to seeing it through.

A reminder of Bihar's strengths

For Sharma, who grew up in Bihar, the recognition carries a more personal meaning. Few places in India can claim the kind of historical and intellectual inheritance that Bihar possesses. Bodh Gaya is where the Buddha attained enlightenment. Vaishali is closely associated with Mahavira. Ancient Pataliputra was the capital of the Mauryan Empire under Ashoka, while Patna is the birthplace of Guru Gobind Singh. Nalanda and Vikramshila were among the great centres of learning in ancient India. Yet Bihar's present-day image often has little to do with this extraordinary history. Its achievements are celebrated in textbooks, but the state has struggled to build contemporary institutions that attract the same admiration.

Sharma drew on an episode from the Ramayana to explain what the museum means to her. Before Hanuman makes his leap across the ocean to Lanka, Jambavan reminds him of the strength he has forgotten. Bihar, she suggested, needed a similar reminder of what it is capable of achieving. The museum offers one. Its galleries house sculptures, coins, manuscripts and artefacts that bring the region's history to life, including the celebrated Didarganj Yakshi. And now, a German travel publication has placed it among the world's ten best museums, ahead of institutions with far longer histories and international reputations. The ranking is one publication's assessment, but it is nevertheless a significant moment for a museum that faced so many questions during its creation.

item.title: Govt clears 12 more proposals worth over Rs 7,500 Cr under electronics components scheme
item.description: The government also launched the Semicon 2.0 web application portal under the ambitious Semicon India Programme.
item.content:encoded:
The government has approved a new tranche of 12 applications, worth over Rs 7,500 crore, under the Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme, IT Secretary S Krishnan said on Friday.

The latest round of approvals also covers projects related to materials and capital goods, widening the scheme's reach across the electronics supply chain.

This round of approvals adds to the momentum behind the scheme, which aims to build a domestic ecosystem for components and reduce India's dependence on imports.

The government is keen to strengthen upstream segments such as raw materials and manufacturing equipment, alongside component production.

The government also launched the Semicon 2.0 web application portal under the ambitious Semicon India Programme.

item.title: MakeMyTrip enters shared mobility space with majority stake in Quick Ride
item.description: MakeMyTrip has acquired the Quick Ride brand and its ride pooling business with a majority stake in this entity.
item.content:encoded:
MakeMyTrip on Friday announced it has acquired a majority stake in 'Quick Ride', a technology-led shared mobility platform, for an undisclosed sum.

The investment provides an opportunity for MakeMyTrip to establish its presence in the shared mobility/ride pooling segment, complementary to the group's existing ground transportation portfolio, the company stated.

Bengaluru-headquartered Quick Ride is a technology-led, asset-light shared mobility platform that connects people travelling along similar routes, enabling affordable ride pooling for everyday commutes.

The 'Quick Ride' brand and its ride pooling business underwent an internal restructuring and are now housed under a new entity, Co Ride Mobility Private Limited. MakeMyTrip has acquired the Quick Ride brand and its ride pooling business with a majority stake in this entity.

Quick Ride's promoters will continue to lead the business. Its erstwhile EV taxi business will remain with the predecessor entity, iDisha Info Labs Private Limited, MakeMyTrip stated.

Rajesh Magow, Co-Founder & Group Chief Executive Officer, MakeMyTrip, said, "As part of our expansion strategy, we have pursued selective strategic partnerships, investments and acquisitions that complement and strengthen our existing business and expand the breadth and depth of our offerings. Ride pooling gives us a presence in high-frequency daily commutes within cities, as well as intercity travel".

Quick Ride will be housed under our ground transport business, and we will bring the learnings from building redBus in India and overseas markets to grow and scale the business, he added.

KNM Rao, Founder and CEO, Quick Ride, said, "Becoming part of the MakeMyTrip group is an important milestone for our team and for the community of users who have placed their trust in us. We look forward to drawing on MakeMyTrip's reach and experience in travel to further scale the business".

In recent years, MakeMyTrip has made acquisitions across travel segments, including Savaari in car rental services, Happay in corporate travel and expense management, Flamingo Transworld in regional group holiday packages and through strategic minority investment in Atlys in visa processing.

item.title: Google Cloud India MD Shashikumar Sreedharan joins Sarvam as President and CBO
item.description: Sreedharan will run Sarvam's business across enterprises and government, and widen its work with digital-native companies, developers and partners.
item.content:encoded:
Sarvam, one of the leading artificial intelligence (AI) startups in India, has announced the appointment of Sashikumar Sreedharan as President and Chief Business Officer. Sreeedharan was previously Managing Director - India of Google Cloud.

A blog post by Sarvam said Sreedharan will also be joining as a board member of the company. His responsibilities include leading the business of Sarvam across enterprises and government, and expanding its work with digital native companies, developers and partners. He will also be responsible for marketing, finance, forward deployed engineering, service delivery, and commercial operations.

“India should be a maker of the intelligence the world runs on. For me, joining Sarvam is a commitment to that opportunity. I look forward to working with the team and our customers to build products that become part of how industries and governments operate,” said Sreedharan.

Sreeedharan has more than three decades of experience building and leading technology businesses. Previously, he led Microsoft India’s enterprise business as the managing director for over five years.

Sarvam said the new appointment comes at a time when the startup is growing in scale and scope. It noted that over 100 enterprises and government institutions are building with Sarvam’s full-stack offering.

“The next phase of Sarvam is about advancing our research, developing products loved by people around the world, and building a company that can operate at a much greater scale. Every enterprise should own its AI,” the blog post said.

Sarvam became a unicorn startup after raising $234 million in the first close of its Series B funding round in June 2026. This round valued the company at $1.5 billion and saw participation from investors such as  HCLTech, Bessemer Venture Partners, Khosla Ventures and Peak XV Partners.

item.title: Artist Bhagya Ajaikumar explains how good curation balances individual expression and collective vision
item.description: In this photo essay, we showcase the ‘Bhoomi’ exhibition at Venkatappa Art Gallery, along with curator insights.
item.content:encoded:
Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,030 posts, we featured an art festival, cartoon gallery. world music festival, telecom expo, millets fair, climate change expo, wildlife conference, startup festival, Diwali rangoli, and jazz festival.

The Venkatappa and Swasti art galleries in Bengaluru recently hosted the group exhibition titled Bhoomi (see our coverage of earlier exhibitions at Venkatappa gallery here). It was curated by Bhagya Ajaikumar and Pradeep Kumar DM, with works by around 40 artists.

The Swasti gallery was launched in Bengaluru in 2007 to promote art and raise funds for the HCG Foundation as support for cancer patients. Since 2018, Swasti has also conducted art therapy events for cancer patients and their family members.

Dedicated art space in a hospital setting gives a positive energy to patients and their family members. With that goal in mind, Swasti has been actively involved in organising art shows, camps and workshops, with artists coming from across the country and abroad.

“I am currently planning and working on several exciting projects, both as an artist and a curator. This includes a solo presentation titled THANDAV, featuring my art creations inspired by classical Indian dance,” Ajaikumar tells YourStory.

The exhibition will be presented at the RASA cultural festival at Prestige Auditorium in Bengaluru, January 8-10. 2027. She is also curating the upcoming third International KALA Symposium in Mysuru.

Also Read
Year in Review: The great Indian consumer reset powered by protein, pickleball and micro-dramas

“With the vision of art as a catalyst for healing and development, the symposium is conceived as a creative platform connecting fine art, healthcare philanthropy, and grassroots community development. It will be hosted at Bharath Cancer Hospital,” she adds.

Her gallery is also planning an art activity with paediatric oncology patients to celebrate Children's Day this month. “Another ongoing initiative is the installation of artworks in consultation rooms across our hospitals,” Ajaikumar says.

As trends in Indian contemporary art, she points to the revival of traditional Indian art forms through contemporary interpretations. “Styles such as Madhubani, Gond, Pichwai and Mysore are being explored through acrylics on canvas, square compositions, minimalistic presentations, and unconventional materials,” she observes.

“With increasing competition and the pressure to produce work within shorter periods, many traditional processes are gradually disappearing. Traditional knowledge and techniques should also be respected,” she affirms.

Another exciting development is the transformation of traditional Indian crafts into large-scale contemporary installations. “Some traditional art forms are moving beyond small-format works on paper to large canvases, murals and public installations,” she says.

Indian contemporary art is also responding to changes in social, political and environmental realities. “Many artists are exploring themes of identity, migration, displacement, urbanisation, globalisation, and ecology. They encourage viewers to question and reflect on the world around them,” Ajaikumar observes.

Also Read
Year in Review: Top 10 celebrity-backed ventures of 2025

“I believe this shift is important because art should not merely be decorative. It can communicate ideas, challenge perceptions and create awareness about issues that affect society,” she affirms.

Collectors are increasingly interested in theme-based series rather than isolated, standalone artworks. “Conceptual works, installations, environmentally conscious practices, and works addressing social and women's issues are receiving greater attention,” she adds.

As for tech trends, AI offers digital artists exciting tools and possibilities for experimentation. “However, use of AI also raises important questions about originality, authorship, authenticity and the value of the human hand and imagination in art,” she cautions.

“Another development I find particularly encouraging is the increasing presence of art in public spaces, especially airports. Major airports in cities such as Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru are providing opportunities to showcase large-scale artworks and installations,” she observes (see our photo essay on art and design at Bengaluru’s airport here).

With their large spaces, airports can bring art closer to people who may not necessarily visit galleries or museums. “These installations often combine art, architecture, unconventional materials, and multimedia practices. They can transform otherwise functional spaces into engaging cultural environments,” she adds.

The exhibitor lineup in her Bhoomi exhibition includes Meenakshi Chinna Rathod, Meghana Gante Ravish, Nagappa Pradhani, Nikhil R Sharma, Nirmala Kumari CS, Premkumar K, Ranganath Amrad, Revanasiddayya SH, Renuka Markande, SG Vasudev, and Santosh Pattar.

Also Read
Year in review: What 2025’s data tells us about women in India

Akshay Bhat is an emerging contemporary artist from Karnataka whose practice reflects an interest in expressive visual language and contemporary aesthetics. Alka Chavda is a contemporary visual artist whose practice centres on painting and mixed media.

Renuka Markande is an accomplished artist, educator and researcher whose creative practice bridges academic inquiry and contemporary visual expression. Bhagya Ajaikumar explores expressive painting and the emotional possibilities of colour and form.

Hanumanta T frequently draws inspiration from local traditions, landscapes and everyday human interactions, transforming familiar imagery into evocative narratives. Ishwarayya OM explores themes of identity, environment and human resilience.

Manushya explores universal themes of humanity, coexistence and personal identity through painting and interdisciplinary practice. Marishamachar draws inspiration from regional narratives and lived experience, and creates works that resonate with both cultural specificity and universal human concerns.

As a curator of such a diverse exhibition, Ajaikumar particularly likes placing emerging artists alongside established professionals. “This allows them to learn from one another and gain greater exposure,” she explains.

“I believe that an exhibition should offer more than a collection of individual artworks. It should create a meaningful visual and intellectual experience for the viewer,” she says.

Also Read
Year in review: startups that raised big from VCs in 2025

This can be particularly challenging when working with a specific theme. “The curator must establish a meaningful connection between the exhibition's concept and the individual artist's interpretation. There should be a common thread connecting their contributions,” she describes.

“Curators also encourage emerging artists and help them develop their ideas. A carefully curated exhibition can challenge younger artists to think beyond their usual boundaries, experiment with new approaches and raise the quality of their work,” Ajaikumar signs off.

Now what have you done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world?

(All photographs taken by Madanmohan Rao on location at Venkatappa Art Gallery.)

item.title: Angel One becomes India's second-largest broker by active clients
item.description: The active client base of Angel One for October was 69.98 lakh which was an addition of 2.43 lakh for the month. Zerodha now is in the third spot.
item.content:encoded:
Financial Services firm Angel One has become the country's second-largest stockbroker in terms of active clients, with 69.98 lakh investors on the National Stock Exchange at the end of October, according to the exchange's latest data.

With an active client base of 69.98 lakh, the brokerage now accounts for 14.97% of 4.67 crore active clients across all brokers on the exchange.

The firm added 2.43 lakh net active clients on NSE in October alone.

Its overall client base reached 4.06 crore at the end of October, up 17.4% year-on-year. The company crossed the 4-crore mark during the month after adding nearly 15 lakh clients in the July-September quarter.

Trading activity also picked up in October, with average daily orders rising 19.6% month-on-month to 69.7 lakh. Gross client additions stood at 6.6 lakh, the highest in nine months.

In terms of the number one position, Groww retained its spot with 1.37 crore active clients for the month of October. It also added the highest number of clients at 3.04 lakh during the month and also Groww’s market share was 29.43%.

Bengaluru headquartered Zerodha slipped to third position with overall 67.59 lakh active clients for the month of October which was down by 32,435 from 67.91 lakh in September. This resulted in Zerodha’s market share slipping to 14.46%.

The growth in client numbers of Angel One came alongside an improvement in financial performance.

Angel One's consolidated revenue from operations rose 18.7% year-on-year to Rs 1,427 crore, and net profit grew 58.2% to Rs 335 crore.

Its wealth management assets under management stood at Rs 16,000 crore at the end of the quarter, up 19.1 per cent sequentially.

item.title: Mamaearth parent Honasa's Q2 net profit rises 87%
item.description: The company reported a net profit of Rs 73.24 crore in Q2FY27. Revenue rose 36% YoY to Rs 731.18 crore.
item.content:encoded:
Honasa Consumer, the parent company of beauty & personal care brand Mamaearth, registered an 87% year-on-year (YoY) rise in net profit for the second quarter of the current fiscal, while revenue rose 36% driven by strong growth across categories.

The company reported a net profit of Rs 73.24 crore in Q2FY27, compared with Rs 39.22 crore in the similar period of FY26. Revenue during the quarter was Rs 731.18 crore, compared with Rs 538.06 crore a year ago.

According to Honasa Consumer, the second quarter revenue growth is the highest it has recorded since its public listing in November 2023.

However, sequentially, profit fell from Rs 90.44 crore in the first quarter. Revenue in the first quarter was Rs 755.94 crore.

Honasa also operates the brands Dermacare and Aqualogica.

CEO Varun Alagh said, “At the brand level, each business is writing its own growth story. Mamaearth has sustained its high-teens growth, The Derma Co. continues to grow profitably. Our Younger Brands grew over 45% YoY, reflecting highlighting the potential of our emerging portfolio.”

He added that each brand has a distinct consumer, proposition and opportunity and the goal is to build a sustainable business in each category.

The omnichannel channel retailer noted that its offline business saw growth, with general trade expanding to over 3.2 lakh outlets and modern trade (large-format retail outlets) recording a 40% YoY growth in offtake.

“As we enter the next phase of growth, we will continue to push the boundaries of innovation, deepen our presence in core categories, and make our products accessible to more consumers across channels,” said Ghazal Alagh, CIO & Co-founder, Honasa Consumer.

For the six months of the fiscal year, the company reported a revenue of Rs 1,487.13 crore, a YoY growth of 31%. The net profit for the period was Rs 163.69 crore, a YoY rise of 103%.

item.title: Delhi HC upholds interim protection for BharatPe’s shareholder rights, dismisses Unity Bank’s appeal
item.description: The court has now, on two occasions, declined to let the bank and its promoter proceed on reserved matters without the prior written consent of RIPL, as the Shareholders’ Agreement (SHA) requires.
item.content:encoded:
A division bench of the Delhi High Court has dismissed an appeal by Unity Bank, upholding the interim protection granted to BharatPe's parent company RIPL (Resilient Innovations Private Limited) under the Shareholders’ Agreement and affirming the order of a single judge.

The court has now, on two occasions, declined to let the bank and its promoter proceed on reserved matters without the prior written consent of RIPL, as the Shareholders’ Agreement (SHA) requires.

Rejecting the bank’s explanation that it had sought RIPL’s consent on Reserved Matters through an “inadvertent error”, the bench called the plea an “argument of desperation and nothing more”. It noted that Unity had expressly sought RIPL’s consent in writing, which showed it knew of the contractual requirement.

The bench reaffirmed that Unity cannot take decisions on Reserved Matters without the prior written consent of RIPL and Centrum, observing that Clause 8 of the SHA explicitly bars any action on such matters without it. It endorsed the single judge’s findings, describing the matter as “elementary”.

The court also rejected Unity’s contention that the Reserve Bank of India had turned down the SHA. It observed that the RBI had never objected to the agreement, which had been submitted to it for approval, and held that the injunction does not obstruct any RBI directive and merely requires enforcement of Clause 8.

Turning down the argument that the SHA cannot override the Articles of Association, the bench noted that Clause 8 opens with a non obstante clause, giving it precedence over the relevant provisions of the Articles.

BharatPe welcomed the decision. A spokesperson said, “The Board must ensure that the Bank complies with the Court’s directions in letter and spirit. We expect the Board to exercise independent judgment, free from undue influence, and act in the interests of the Bank and all its stakeholders, including minority shareholders. Governance processes followed since the Bank’s inception must be respected and applied consistently. They cannot be set aside to favour one shareholder group at the expense of another.

“We expect the Board to guide the Bank in honouring its contractual obligations and ensuring that its actions comply with the Court’s directions. We believe the Hon’ble Division Bench’s decision reinforces the importance of the agreed governance framework and the shareholder rights that formed the basis of the joint venture in 2021. Respect for these commitments is essential to maintaining trust between shareholders and protecting the institution’s long-term interests.”

The ruling reinforces that Unity Bank is bound by the Reserved Matter provisions of the SHA and cannot dismiss its own written requests for shareholder consent as inadvertent errors to avoid its contractual obligations.
